problem: Prior semantic mapping work assigned labels from closed vocabularies to metric maps, so robots could not handle novel objects, open-ended language or flexible human-robot interaction; the literature on open-vocabulary mapping built on foundation models is also fragmented.
motivation: Robots coexisting with humans need semantic maps that can be queried in natural language. LLMs, VLMs and generative 3D representations (NeRF, 3D Gaussian splatting) have made this possible, so the field needs a structured overview linking mapping to navigation and planning.
key_idea: A survey that organizes open-vocabulary semantic mapping into a four-part taxonomy (3D metric map feature fusion, object-centric, hierarchical scene graph, continuous generative 3D language fields) and connects it to foundation-model-based navigation.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablations or experimental analysis can be cited. The abstract's takeaway is that representation choice (dense features, objects, scene graphs, language fields) determines how language-accessible the map is for downstream navigation and task planning.
method: Taxonomy: four categories: (i) fusion of semantic features into 3D metric maps, (ii) object-centric open-vocabulary representations, (iii) hierarchical scene graphs, (iv) continuous generative 3D language fields (NeRF / 3DGS).
Historical review: revisits the history of open-vocabulary semantic mapping.
Navigation overview: covers foundation-model navigation with language-accessible maps, from object-goal navigation to LLM-based hierarchical task planning.
Resources: introduces evaluation datasets, simulators, robot platforms and metrics.
Open challenges: summarizes seven open challenges.
numbers_note: abstract only; the paper is a survey and reports no experiments
results: This is a review with no experimental results. It contributes a four-part taxonomy, a history, a navigation overview, a summary of datasets, simulators, platforms and metrics, and seven open challenges.
limitations: Only the abstract was available, so details of coverage and the seven challenges are unknown.
As a survey, it has no new method or empirical comparison.
